passages.original: post hunc Numa Pompilius Marti et Robigini fecit (nam et robiginis deam finxerunt); dehinc Tullus Hostilius, dehinc Ancus Martius et ceteri. qui quos quem per ordinem et quibus idolis ludos instituerint, positumum est apud Suetonium Tranquillum uel a quibus Tranquillus accepit. sed haec satis erunt ad originis de idololatria reatum.
passages.english: After him Numa Pompilius held [games] for Mars and Robigo (for they also invented a goddess of blight); then Tullus Hostilius, then Ancus Martius and the rest. Who these were, and in what order, and for which idols they instituted games, is set out in Suetonius Tranquillus, or in those from whom Tranquillus received it. But this will be enough to establish the guilt of [the games'] origin in idolatry.
passages.notes: "Robigini" is the dative of Robigo/Robigus, the deity of blight (rust) in grain; the parenthesis puns on "robigo" (blight). The phrase "qui quos quem per ordinem" appears garbled; it is translated as "who these were, and in what order." "positumum" is taken as a scanning error for "positum" (set out).

passages.original: res equestris retro simplex: de dorso agebatur, et utique communis usus; reus non erat. sed cum ad ludos coactus est, transiit a dei munere ad daemoniorum officia. itaque Castori et Polluci deputatur, haec species, quibus equos a Mercurio distributos Stesichorus docet. sed et Neptunus equestris est, quem Graeci ἵππιον appellant. seiugas uero Ioui, quadrigas Soli, bigas Lunae sanxerunt. sed et Primus Erichthonius currus et quattuor ausus Iungere equos rapidusque rotis insistere uictor.
passages.english: Horsemanship was formerly a simple thing: it was done from horseback, and was certainly of common use; it was not guilty [of anything]. But when it was forced into the games, it passed over from being a gift of God to the service of demons. And so this kind [of spectacle] is assigned to Castor and Pollux, to whom, as Stesichorus teaches, horses were allotted by Mercury. But Neptune too is equestrian; the Greeks call him *Hippios* ["of horses"]. And they consecrated the six-horse team to Jupiter, the four-horse team to the Sun, the two-horse team to the Moon. But also: "Erichthonius first dared to yoke chariots and four horses, and to stand victorious upon swift wheels."
passages.notes: The phrase "haec species" is awkwardly placed in the text as transmitted and may be corrupt; it is taken here as the subject ("this kind [of spectacle]"). The verse quotation is from Virgil, Georgics 3.113–114. "Seiugas" is read as "seiuges/seiugas", six-horse chariots.
